thread.title_full: McKee picks Matos, not Shekarchi, to fill RI Supreme Court seat - NewsBreak

author: Alexandra Leslie
title: McKee picks Matos, not Shekarchi, to fill RI Supreme Court seat - NewsBreak
text:
By Alexandra Leslie Ted Nesi Shaun Towne ,
12 hours ago
PROVIDENCE, R.I. (WPRI) — Former House Speaker Joe Shekarchi won’t be the next justice on the R.I. Supreme Court, Gov. Dan McKee announced Wednesday, after months of controversy over the lawmaker’s effort to get the seat.
At a State House news conference, McKee announced he has picked R.I. Superior Court Judge Luis Matos as his nominee for the seat. A former assistant U.S. attorney, Matos was first appointed to the bench in 2012 by then-Gov. Lincoln Chafee.
Matos, 62, was born in Batalha, Portugal, and immigrated to Rhode Island in 1969. He grew up in the Fox Point neighborhood of Providence and became the first person in his family to graduate from college, attending Brown University and then the University of Connecticut School of Law. (He is not related to Lt. Gov. Sabina Matos.)
McKee said he had engaged in “careful vetting” of all the candidates before making his pick, and was impressed with Matos’s background and qualifications. The other candidates were state prosecutor Christopher Bush, Family Court Judge Laureen D’Ambra, and attorney John Roberts.
In a joint statement, House Speaker Chris Blazejewski and Senate President Val Lawson said they will not take up the nomination until after the Nov. 3 general election.
“We informed the governor of our shared goal of taking the politics as much as possible out of what has become an overly politicized Supreme Court nomination process,” the two legislative leaders said. “We do not believe it is appropriate or prudent for consideration of any nominee, regardless of who it is, to begin until after that date.”
Shekarchi stepped down as speaker in May, and his application to fill the court vacancy — created by the retirement of Justice Maureen McKenna Goldberg — has triggered a major ethics battle.
A complaint was filed with the R.I. Ethics Commission accusing Shekarchi of violating the state’s revolving-door rules, but Shekarchi went to court and secured a favorable ruling from Judge Richard Licht . The Judicial Nominating Commission then sent Shekarchi’s name to the governor along with the others, a move that itself stirred controversy when it emerged that commission members who voted for Shekarchi had donated over $30,000 to him.
The ethics fight isn’t over, despite McKee not choosing Shekarchi for the nomination.
On Tuesday, the commission’s executive director and chief prosecutor, Jason Gramitt, filed an appeal of Licht’s decision to the R.I. Supreme Court.
“The last few months have shown us that this is a significant issue of great public concern, likely to repeat itself,” Gramitt said. “Therefore, it is appropriate and necessary to continue the appeal to bring the matter to our highest court for a final resolution.”
In an email, Shekarchi shared a brief statement on the nomination.
“I want to congratulate Judge Matos on his nomination by the governor,” Shekarchi said. “I also want to thank everyone who supported my candidacy for the Supreme Court.”
A 12 News/Emerson College poll in May found voters were skeptical about Shekarchi’s candidacy, with 36% opposed to his appointment and only 21% in favor. But nearly half — 44% — had no opinion.
Two of the Shekarchi bid’s most vocal critics, Common Cause Rhode Island executive director John Marion and former Roger Williams School of Law Dean Michael Yelnosky, both praised the decision to name Matos but expressed continued concern over recent events.
“The saga of Representative Shekarchi’s application for the Supreme Court, even though it was unsuccessful in this instance, has shined a light on serious problems with our ethics, judicial selection, and campaign finance systems in Rhode Island,” Marion said in a statement. He said his group would be “championing reforms” to state government in light of what had happened.
Unlike other states, Rhode Island has no mandatory retirement age for judges. But legal observers expect additional vacancies on the Supreme Court in the coming years due to the advanced ages of two justices, 77-year-old Chief Justice Paul Suttell and 86-year-old Associate Justice William P. Robinson.
